questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Why we are drawn to reading bad news
How to find good news online
The best news websites
How phones damage our eyes
questions.why: Neil says they'll investigate why we feel compelled to look at, and even seek out, bad news.

questions.q: How does Neil feel about doomscrolling?
options: He never does it and doesn't understand it
He enjoys it very much in the evenings
He hates to admit he sometimes does it
He does it all day, even at work
questions.why: He says, 'I hate to admit it, but I do sometimes doomscroll.'

questions.q: What did research from the University of California find?
options: Only young people in rich countries doomscroll
People everywhere doomscroll, whatever culture
Doomscrolling is most common in the USA
Doomscrolling makes most people happier
questions.why: It found people all over the world doomscroll, regardless of culture.

questions.q: What two possible causes does Ella al-Shamahi ask about?
options: Boredom and loneliness in modern life
Work stress and a lack of good sleep
Social media and too much advertising
24/7 news on phones, or an old instinct
questions.why: She asks if it's '24/7 doom on tap on our phones' or a compulsion from 'way, way back'.

questions.q: According to the theory of 'negativity bias', why do humans pay attention to bad news?
options: Knowing about danger helped us survive
Bad news is far more common than good news
Journalists prefer to write bad news stories
It makes us feel better about our own lives
questions.why: Neil says knowing the dangers was vital to survival, so we naturally pay attention to negative things.

questions.q: What difference between cave people and us does Ella describe?
options: Cave people had much more bad news to deal with
Cave people only heard local bad news
Cave people never shared news with others
Cave people only ever heard good news
questions.why: She says a neighbour's cave would only know the bad news from that particular mountain.

questions.q: What does Clara Amfo think about how society sees negative experiences?
options: It ignores them
It fears them too much
It makes them sound better than they are
It talks about them too little
questions.why: She says trauma is romanticised and we believe negative experiences shape us more than joyful ones.

questions.q: What does Neil conclude about stopping doomscrolling?
options: It is very easy to do
It is not necessary
It is only possible for older people
It might be best, but it's not easy
questions.why: He says maybe it's best to stop, but with so much bad news pouring in, it's not easy.
